A pestilence is a deadly, highly contagious disease that spreads rapidly and kills enormous numbers of people across a wide area. Think of it as the most catastrophic, civilization-shaking form of illness imaginable — one that doesn't just make individuals sick, but sweeps through entire towns, regions, or whole countries, leaving mass death in its wake.

The defining power of the word comes from three qualities working together: it is fatal, it is contagious, and it is widespread. Remove any one of those three, and you're no longer describing a pestilence. A common cold is contagious and widespread but not deadly. Cancer is deadly and widespread but not contagious. A pestilence is all three at once — and that combination is what makes it so uniquely devastating.
What it looks like in practice

The clearest examples come from history. The Black Death of the 14th century, which wiped out roughly a third of Europe's population. Smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people over centuries before it was finally eradicated. Cholera outbreaks that swept through entire continents in the 1800s. These are the kinds of events the word "pestilence" was made to describe — events so catastrophic they literally altered the course of human civilization.

So when you use the word "pestilence," you are not describing an ordinary illness, or even a moderately bad outbreak. You are describing something at the most extreme, horrifying end of the scale.

Like many powerful words, pestilence has grown beyond its original medical meaning. It is also used figuratively to describe anything that spreads harmfully through society the way a deadly disease does — corrupting, destroying, or consuming whatever it touches.

For example: "Hatred is a pestilence that, left unchecked, will consume an entire nation." Hatred isn't literally a disease, but the word "pestilence" works because it captures how such things spread invisibly, grow beyond control, and cause mass destruction. Writers and speakers choose this word when they want to communicate that something is not just bad, but systemically devastating.
How it compares to similar words

Understanding how pestilence relates to nearby words will sharpen your grasp of it.

An epidemic is a disease spreading rapidly in a community or region. It doesn't have to be fatal — a widespread flu season can be called an epidemic. A pandemic is simply an epidemic that has gone global. Neither word, on its own, implies the mass death and catastrophic scale that pestilence does.

Plague is probably the closest word to pestilence, and the two are often used interchangeably. However, plague carries extra meanings pestilence does not: it can describe an infestation of animals or insects ("a plague of locusts"), and it is also the clinical name for a specific bacterial disease (bubonic plague). Pestilence stays purely in the territory of deadly, widespread disease — or its figurative equivalent.

Pestilence is not a casual, everyday word. Nobody says "I've come down with a pestilence." It belongs to formal writing, literature, history, and religion. You will find it in the Bible, where it repeatedly appears as one of the gravest divine punishments. You'll find it in classic literature, in historical accounts of major outbreaks, and in serious journalism about catastrophic events.

This gives the word a uniquely dark and solemn quality. When a writer chooses "pestilence" over a more neutral word like "disease" or "outbreak," it is a deliberate choice to evoke doom, magnitude, and moral gravity. The word doesn't just describe — it makes you feel the weight of what it's describing.

In its literal sense: "The pestilence spread through the city so swiftly that physicians were overwhelmed before they could even name the disease." / "The pestilence of the 14th century reshaped European society in ways that took generations to understand."

In its figurative sense: "He called corruption a pestilence eating away at the foundations of government." / "Misinformation is the pestilence of the digital age, spreading faster than any correction can contain it."

A pestilence is a deadly, contagious disease that kills large numbers of people across a wide area — and figuratively, anything that spreads through society causing widespread, devastating harm. It is always a word of scale, severity, and dread.
